entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Julie Charpentier (1770–1845) was a French sculptor active in the Revolutionary and Napoleonic decades, when a small number of women gained Salon visibility in a field still dominated by male academy structures. She produced portrait busts and ideal works that entered the exhibition culture of Paris during regime upheavals that both disrupted and occasionally opened artistic careers.

Women sculptors faced barriers in life-class access, large-stone workshop culture, and state commissions, so Charpentier’s professional presence itself is historically notable. Her work participates in the broader neoclassical portrait market that served families and officials seeking marble or plaster likenesses.

Feminist and institutional art histories cite her among early modern French women who claimed space in sculpture before the later nineteenth-century expansion of female art education.
